usage: goes before the 안 of negation
examples: 저는 김치를 자주 먹어요.
I eat kimchi often.
Simple habit: 자주 sits directly before the verb 먹어요.
요즘 친구를 자주 못 만나요.
These days I can't meet my friends often.
Everyday: with 못, 자주 still comes first — 자주 못 만나요, not 못 자주.
이 동네는 버스가 자주 안 와서 불편해요.
In this neighborhood the bus doesn't come often, so it's inconvenient.
Real situation: 자주 안 와요 = 'comes rarely'; the adverb hugs the whole negated verb.
nuance: 자주 means 'often / frequently' and describes how many TIMES an action repeats over a period — it answers 얼마나 자주 ('how often'), never how fast or how well. The frequency scale runs 항상(always) > 자주(often) > 가끔(sometimes) > 거의 안(hardly), and 자주 sits high but short of 'always'. Its natural opposite is 가끔; learners confuse 자주 with 빨리(quickly), but 자주 is about count of occurrences while 빨리 is about speed of one action — 빨리 먹어요 means 'eats fast', 자주 먹어요 means 'eats often'. Register-neutral, fine for everyone. The big English-speaker pitfall is word order: English lets you say 'I go there often' with the adverb last, but Korean glues 자주 immediately before the verb (자주 가요), and even before 안/못 in negatives (자주 안 가요).

mistakes: Saying 가요 자주 by copying English 'I go often'. Korean adverbs precede the verb, so it must be 자주 가요.

usage: I go once in a while
examples: 저는 가끔 라면을 먹어요.
I sometimes eat ramyeon.
Simple: 가끔 marks a low-frequency habit, sitting before 먹어요.
주말에는 가끔 늦잠을 자요.
On weekends I sometimes sleep in.
Everyday: pairs naturally with 주말에는 to mean 'on some weekends, not all'.
바쁘지만 가끔은 부모님께 전화를 드려요.
I'm busy, but every so often I call my parents.
Real situation: 가끔은 (with 은) softly contrasts 'at least sometimes' against the busyness.
nuance: 가끔 means 'sometimes / once in a while / occasionally' — clearly less frequent than 자주 but more than 거의 안(hardly ever): the scale is 항상 > 자주 > 가끔 > 거의 안 > 전혀 안. Its nearest rival is 때때로, which means the same but is more bookish/written; in everyday speech 가끔 is the natural choice, while 때때로 can sound like an essay. You can intensify it as 가끔씩 ('every now and then'), which feels even more sporadic and warm. Register-neutral and safe with anyone. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, word order — it must precede the verb (가끔 가요, not 가요 가끔); second, learners over-reach and use 가끔 for things that are actually frequent, so calibrate it as 'only occasionally', not 'fairly often'.

usage: 100% of the time, before the verb
examples: 언니는 항상 아침을 먹어요.
My older sister always eats breakfast.
Simple: 항상 = every single time, with no exception, before 먹어요.
저는 항상 핸드폰을 손에 들고 다녀요.
I always carry my phone in my hand.
Everyday: 항상 stresses an unbroken habit; pairs well with 들고 다니다 ('carry around').
늘 건강하시고 항상 행복하세요.
Stay healthy and always be happy.
Real situation: a warm blessing — here 늘 and 항상 are swapped freely; both mean 'always'.
nuance: 항상 (Sino-Korean 恒常, 恒 'constant' + 常 'usual', literally 'constant-usual') means 'always / at all times', marking an action that holds without exception — far stronger than 보통(usually), which allows exceptions. Its near-synonym is 늘, a pure native word with the same meaning; the two are almost always interchangeable, though 늘 feels a touch softer and warmer (common in well-wishes) while 항상 sounds a hair more emphatic and is slightly more frequent in writing. Another cousin, 언제나, leans poetic/literary. All are register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 항상 to mean 'usually' — English 'always' is loose ('I'm always late-ish'), but Korean 항상 is literally 100%, so for a normal-but-not-absolute habit use 보통, and keep the word before the verb (항상 와요, not 와요 항상).

Word-order slip: 와요 항상 copies English. Korean needs 항상 와요, adverb before verb.
Assuming 항상 and 늘 differ in meaning and over-thinking which to pick. They are interchangeable; just keep one register — both are neutral and natural.

usage: here 보통 works as a noun/modifier
examples: 저는 보통 일곱 시에 일어나요.
I usually get up at seven.
Simple: 보통 = 'as a rule, with exceptions allowed', before 일어나요.
점심은 보통 회사 근처에서 먹어요.
I usually eat lunch near the office.
Everyday: describes the default choice, not an absolute rule.
보통은 안 그런데 오늘은 좀 피곤하네요.
Usually I'm not like this, but today I'm a bit tired.
Real situation: 보통은 (with 은) sets up a contrast — 'normally... but today...'.
nuance: 보통 (Sino-Korean 普通, 普 'widespread' + 通 'common', literally 'widely-common') means 'usually / normally / ordinarily' and frames what happens as a rule WHILE leaving room for exceptions — that exception-tolerance is exactly what separates it from 항상(always, no exceptions). Think of the ladder 항상 > 보통 > 자주 > 가끔: 보통 says 'this is my default'. Uniquely among these adverbs, 보통 is also a noun/adjective meaning 'ordinary' (보통 사람 'an average person', 보통이에요 'it's so-so'), so context tells you which use is active. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'usually' as a soft 'always' and over-claiming — if you truly mean every time, use 항상; and as always, keep the adverb before the verb (보통 가요), not after.

examples: 저는 보통 일찍 자요.
I usually sleep early.
Simple: 일찍 = at an early hour, before 자요.
내일은 일찍 일어나고 싶어요.
Tomorrow I want to get up early.
Everyday: 일찍 + 일어나다 is the standard 'wake up early' collocation.
길이 막힐까 봐 30분 일찍 출발했어요.
Worried about traffic, I left thirty minutes early.
Real situation: 일찍 here means 'ahead of schedule', and 30분 일찍 = 'earlier by 30 min'.
nuance: 일찍 means 'early' in the sense of an EARLY POINT IN TIME — early hour of the day or ahead of a schedule — and is the natural opposite of 늦게(late). The classic confusion is 일찍 vs 빨리: 일찍 is about WHEN on the clock (일찍 일어나요 = 'wake up at an early hour'), while 빨리 is about SPEED/quickness (빨리 일어나요 = 'get up quick!'). So '일찍 오세요' invites someone to arrive at an early time, whereas '빨리 오세요' urges them to hurry. It pairs habitually with 자다, 일어나다, 출근하다, 도착하다, 출발하다. Register-neutral and polite-safe. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 일찍/빨리 mix-up, since English 'early' and 'fast/quick' feel adjacent but map to two different Korean adverbs; also remember 일찍 is an adverb already, so you never conjugate it like the adjective 이르다.

Trying to conjugate it as if it were an adjective. 일찍 is the fixed adverb; you don't say 일찍어요. The related adjective is 이르다 ('to be early').
Word order: 와요 일찍 mirrors English; Korean puts the adverb first — 일찍 와요.

examples: 어제 너무 늦게 잤어요.
I went to bed too late yesterday.
Simple: 늦게 = at a late hour, here intensified by 너무.
주말에는 늦게까지 자요.
On weekends I sleep in until late.
Everyday: 늦게까지 ('until late') is a high-frequency collocation.
회의가 길어져서 어제 늦게까지 일했어요.
The meeting ran long, so I worked late yesterday.
Real situation: 늦게 describes finishing at a late hour, the opposite of 일찍 끝내다.
nuance: 늦게 means 'late', i.e. at a LATE POINT IN TIME or behind schedule, and is the exact opposite of 일찍(early). It is the adverbial form of the adjective 늦다('to be late'), built by attaching -게 to the stem 늦- (늦- + -게 → 늦게); this -게 ending is the general Korean machine for turning a descriptive verb into an adverb. The everyday combo 늦게까지 means 'until late' (늦게까지 공부해요 'study until late'). Two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) keep the -게 — 늦게 is the adverb, while 늦어요 is the conjugated sentence-ending 'is/am late', and 늦은 is the noun-modifier 'late ~'; dropping the -게 and saying 늦어 자요 is wrong. (2) Don't confuse lateness-in-time with slowness — 늦게 가요 means 'go at a late time', whereas 천천히 가요 means 'go slowly'. Register-neutral.

Confusing 늦게 (late in time) with 천천히 (slowly). 늦게 와요 = 'arrive late'; 천천히 와요 = 'come slowly / take your time'.
Using the modifier 늦은 where an adverb is needed. 늦은 means 'late ~' before a noun (늦은 밤 'late night'); before a verb you need 늦게.

usage: please go ahead / do it first
examples: 저 먼저 갈게요.
I'll head off first.
Simple: 먼저 = ahead of others in time/order, before 갈게요.
손을 먼저 씻고 밥을 먹어요.
Wash your hands first, then eat.
Everyday: 먼저 marks step one of a sequence (먼저 A 하고 B).
먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.
I'll be heading in/out first (leaving before you).
Real situation: a polite set phrase to excuse yourself before colleagues — 'I'll go ahead.'
nuance: 먼저 means 'first / beforehand / ahead (of others)' — it ranks one action or person EARLIER in a sequence or in time. The key contrast is 먼저 vs 처음: 먼저 is relative ('before the other thing/person', e.g. 먼저 가요 'go ahead of you'), while 처음 means 'the first time ever / the beginning' (처음 만나요 'meeting for the first time'). So 먼저 봤어요 = 'I saw it first (before you)', but 처음 봤어요 = 'I saw it for the first time'. 먼저 is also a courtesy word: 먼저 가세요 / 먼저 하세요 ('go ahead, you first') is everyday politeness, and 먼저 갈게요 / 먼저 들어가겠습니다 softens leaving before others. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping every 'first' to one word — choose 먼저 for order-relative 'first/ahead', but 처음 for 'first-ever/at first', and keep 먼저 before the verb.

Conversely, using 먼저 for 'the first time'. 먼저 만나요 means 'meet first (before others)'; 'meet for the first time' is 처음 만나요.
Placing it after the verb. English 'you go first' tempts 가요 먼저; Korean order is 먼저 가요 (or politely 먼저 가세요).

examples: 벌써 점심시간이에요?
Is it lunchtime already?
Simple: 벌써 voices surprise that time passed fast.
그 책을 벌써 다 읽었어요.
I've already finished that book.
Everyday: with past tense + 다, 벌써 stresses 'done sooner than expected'.
눈이 벌써 녹았네요. 봄인가 봐요.
The snow has already melted. It must be spring.
Real situation: 벌써 + the surprise-marker -네요 conveys mild astonishment.
nuance: 벌써 means 'already', but its core flavor is SURPRISE that something happened sooner than you expected — 'wow, already?'. Compare its near-twin 이미: 이미 is the neutral 'already / by now' that simply reports a completed fact (이미 끝났어요 'it's already finished', stating it), whereas 벌써 adds the emotional jolt (벌써 끝났어요? 'it's done already?!'). So a flat report prefers 이미; an astonished reaction prefers 벌써. It naturally rides with past tense and with 다('all'), and often co-occurs with the exclamatory endings -네요/-군요. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't pair 벌써 with the future — English 'already' can sit oddly with plans, but 벌써 is about something that has ALREADY occurred, so it takes past/completed verbs (벌써 갔어요), not 벌써 갈 거예요. Use 곧/이미 곧 logic for 'soon' instead.

usage: there's still a long way to go
examples: 저는 아직 학생이에요.
I'm still a student.
Simple: with a positive noun-sentence, 아직 = 'still'.
밥을 아직 안 먹었어요.
I haven't eaten yet.
Everyday: 아직 + 안/못 + past = 'not yet'; the most common pattern.
거의 다 됐어요? 아니요, 아직이요.
Almost done? — No, not yet.
Real situation: 아직 can stand alone as 아직이요 ('not yet') in reply.
nuance: 아직 covers both 'still' and 'not yet', and which one surfaces depends on polarity: with a POSITIVE verb it means 'still' (아직 자요 'still sleeping'), and with a NEGATIVE verb it means 'not yet' (아직 안 잤어요 'haven't slept yet'). It is the natural counterpart to 벌써/이미 — 아직 안 끝났어요 ('not finished yet') is the mirror of 벌써 끝났어요 ('already finished'). It often rides with the ongoing form -고 있다 to stress an action in progress (아직 자고 있어요 'still sleeping right now') and shows up in fixed phrases like 아직 멀었어요 ('still a long way off'). Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the 아직/벌써 confusion and the negation logic: because English 'yet' lives in questions/negatives, learners forget that Korean 아직 itself flips meaning with the verb's polarity — pair 아직 with 안/못 to say 'not yet', and use it with a plain positive verb to say 'still'.

Register-neutral.
It is the natural counterpart to 벌써/이미 — 아직 안 끝났어요 ('not finished yet') is the mirror of 벌써 끝났어요 ('already finished').

The English-speaker pitfall is the 아직/벌써 confusion and the negation logic: because English 'yet' lives in questions/negatives, learners forget that Korean 아직 itself flips meaning with the verb's polarity — pair 아직 with 안/못 to say 'not yet', and use it with a plain positive verb to say 'still'.

mistakes: Confusing 아직 with 벌써. 아직 안 왔어요 = 'hasn't come yet'; 벌써 왔어요 = 'already came'. They point in opposite directions.
Trying to say 'not yet' with a positive verb. 아직 먹었어요 reads as 'still ate' and is odd; you need the negative: 아직 안 먹었어요.
Adding -았/었- when the state still holds. For 'I'm still hungry' say 아직 배고파요 (present), not 아직 배고팠어요; the past tense would mean the hunger is already over, which contradicts 아직.

examples: 내일 또 만나요.
Let's meet again tomorrow.
Simple: 또 = 'one more time', a friendly repeat before 만나요.
또 늦었어? 어제도 늦었잖아.
Late again? You were late yesterday too.
Everyday: 또 here carries a tone of 'yet again', mild reproach.
맛있었어요. 다음에 또 올게요!
It was delicious. I'll come again next time!
Real situation: 또 in a warm farewell; 또 올게요 / 또 봬요 are set goodbyes.
nuance: 또 means 'again / once more', and by extension 'also/additionally'; it marks an action REPEATING. Its near-synonym is 다시, and the dividing line matters: 또 is a plain repetition or recurrence ('one more time', often emotional — delight in 또 봐요 or annoyance in 또?!), while 다시 leans toward 'again, properly / from the start / anew', as in redoing something (다시 하세요 'do it over (correctly)'). So 또 전화할게요 = 'I'll call again (next time)', but 다시 전화할게요 = 'I'll call back / try again'. 또 is the natural word in casual goodbyes (또 봐요, 또 만나요) and in venting (또 그래 'there you go again'). Register-neutral, very colloquial-friendly. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting every 'again' to one word — use 또 for casual recurrence/'see you again', 다시 for 'redo/anew', and keep it before the verb.

mistakes: Reaching for 다시 in a casual goodbye. 다시 봐요 is understandable but leans 'meet again (to pick things back up)'; the warm, idiomatic 'see you again' Koreans actually say is 또 봐요 / 또 만나요.
Using 또 when you mean 'do it over correctly'. 또 하세요 = 'do it one more time'; to mean 'redo it properly / from scratch' say 다시 하세요.
Word order: 와요 또 echoes English 'come again'; Korean puts the adverb first — 또 와요.

usage: I love it / it's so good
examples: 이 신발은 너무 작아요.
These shoes are too small.
Simple: classic 'excessive' use — 너무 + adjective = beyond the right amount.
어제 커피를 너무 많이 마셨어요.
I drank too much coffee yesterday.
Everyday: 너무 stacks onto 많이 ('a lot') to mean 'too much'.
와, 이 케이크 너무 맛있어요!
Wow, this cake is so delicious!
Real situation: in casual speech 너무 flips positive, meaning 'so/really', not 'excessively'.
nuance: 너무 literally means 'too / excessively' — past the appropriate point, usually a complaint (너무 비싸요 'too expensive', 너무 매워요 'too spicy'). The textbook contrast is 너무 vs 아주: 아주 is a neutral intensifier ('very', no judgment), while 너무 traditionally signals EXCESS (a problem). BUT in modern colloquial Korean, 너무 has drifted into a positive 'so/super' (너무 좋아요 'I love it', 너무 예뻐요 'so pretty') — so tone and context decide whether it's a complaint or enthusiasm. It also fossilizes into the verb 너무하다 ('to be too much / go overboard', e.g. 너무해요 'that's not fair'). Register: the positive sense is casual/spoken; in formal writing keep 너무 for genuine excess and use 매우/아주 for neutral emphasis. The English-speaker pitfall: don't assume 너무 is always negative like English 'too' — in speech 너무 좋다 is a compliment, and for plain neutral 'very' before an adjective, 아주/매우 is safer in formal contexts.

mistakes: Reading every 너무 as the negative 'too'. 너무 좋아요 in conversation means 'I really love it', not 'I like it too much'.
Using 너무 for neutral 'very' in formal writing. There 너무 still implies excess; prefer 매우 or 아주 for plain emphasis.
Forgetting 너무하다 is a real verb. 너무해요 means 'that's too much / that's unfair', not a typo — it's 너무 used predicatively.

usage: 아주 can even scale another adverb
examples: 이 빵은 아주 맛있어요.
This bread is very tasty.
Simple: 아주 = plain 'very', no nuance of excess, before 맛있어요.
그분은 한국어를 아주 잘해요.
That person speaks Korean very well.
Everyday: 아주 + 잘하다 cleanly means 'very well', a neutral compliment.
이건 아주 중요한 문제예요.
This is a very important matter.
Real situation: in writing/formal speech 아주 is the safe, judgment-free intensifier.
nuance: 아주 means 'very / quite' — a NEUTRAL degree intensifier that simply turns the dial up without implying anything is excessive. That neutrality is the whole point of 아주 vs 너무: 너무 traditionally flags excess ('too much, a problem'), while 아주 just emphasizes (아주 비싸요 = 'very expensive' as a fact; 너무 비싸요 = 'too expensive', a complaint). Its close formal cousin is 매우, which means the same 'very' but sounds more written/bookish; in everyday speech 아주 (or casual 정말/진짜) is more natural, and 매우 shines in essays and news. 아주 sits before adjectives, descriptive verbs, and even other adverbs (아주 잘, 아주 많이). Register-neutral and safe with anyone, including formal contexts. The English-speaker pitfall is over-defaulting to 너무 for 'very' (because learners hear it constantly in casual speech) — when you want a clean, judgment-free 'very', especially in polite or written Korean, reach for 아주 or 매우.
